The page header reads 'W3C Recommendation 16 April 2002 obsoleted 30 August 2018'. The obsoletion version is TR/2018/OBSL-P3P-20180830.

The notes misstate W3C's reason. 'A machine-readable policy nobody enforced' is not what W3C says. The obsoletion notice gives insufficient ecosystem uptake as the reason: fewer than 6% of the top 10,000 sites, and 'No current (2018) user agents' interpreting or acting on P3P policies. The word 'current' matters, because in the 2000s Internet Explorer's cookie filtering did act on P3P compact policies. So 'nobody enforced' overstates the case.
Caveat for the page: the BuiltWith figure counts sites that 'support' P3P, which in practice largely means sending compact-policy headers. It measures deployment, not accurate or honoured policies.

fieldFixes.notes: W3C's stated reason for obsoleting P3P on 30 Aug 2018 was too little uptake: fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most-visited sites supported it, and no browser still in use in 2018 interpreted or acted on P3P policies. It was a machine-readable privacy policy from the site's side, with no agreement from the person.

issues: All three quotes are verbatim. On 2026-09-23 I fetched the FAQ and IEEE pages fresh and fetched w3.org/TR/tracking-dnt/ with curl (the helper gets 403); every --check returned FOUND.

The correction's description of DNT overstates the case. The W3C DNT Note's own abstract says it 'also defines mechanisms for sites to communicate whether and how they honor a received preference', including a tracking-status resource and the Tk response header, plus APIs for user-granted exceptions. So DNT did include a site response and exceptions stored in the browser. What it lacked was a signed agreement and a matching record kept by both sides. 'No agreement or record' should be narrowed.

Two sub-claims had no source on the record: that browsers or plug-ins may carry the signal as a header like DNT and GPC, and that the W3C working group closed for lack of deployment. Both are now sourced, from the MyTerms FAQ and the DNT Note's status section. Note that the FAQ misspells 'Global Privacy Conrol' [sic], so the correction paraphrases it rather than quoting.
'Public roster' is loose. The standard says the roster is 'kept by an independent and neutral non-business entity'.

fieldFixes.correction: Browsers or plug-ins may carry the signal; the MyTerms FAQ mentions browser headers on the model of Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control. But IEEE 7012 is about a contract. The person proffers a standard-form agreement from a roster kept by a neutral non-business body, and the organisation accepts it. Both sign electronically, and both keep matching records for audit or dispute. DNT was a one-way preference. Sites could answer with a tracking-status signal and browsers could store user-granted exceptions, but nothing was signed and no matching record was kept by both sides. Its W3C working group concluded its work in January 2019 for lack of deployment.

fieldFixes.correction: Cookie banners and consent-management platforms present the organisation's choices to the person. Under MyTerms the person presents terms and the organisation agrees. MyData calls the default 'Service Delivery Only' agreement (SD-BASE) the direct equivalent of 'Strictly Necessary Only', but expressed by the person before any banner can be shown. The MyTerms FAQ allows that tech from consent tools might prove useful in building MyTerms ceremonies and compliance audits. The 2017 PAR says the standard does not address privacy policies, because they are one-sided and need no agreement.

issues: All three quotes are verbatim. On 2026-09-23 I fetched the IEEE page fresh, and fetched the projectvrm.org and doc.searls.com posts with curl (the helper gets 403); every --check returned FOUND. The ProjectVRM post is titled 'The MyTerms PAR' and is dated April 6, 2025.

'The form of the shared record is left open' had no source on the record. The MyTerms FAQ says it directly: 'This is an option left open by the MyTerms standard, to maximize development choices'. The claim that the MyTerms Agreement Record is only an idea is supported by Searls: 'Note that this is something I just made up'. His POC post also floats a blockchain log only 'to attract developers who are fond of those'.

The correction slightly overstates the standard's neutrality. The standard does impose requirements: an agreed contract 'shall be signed electronically by both parties or their agents' and 'a matching record shall be kept by both sides'. Neutral on technology is not the same as requiring nothing. I have added this to the correction.

Caveat: the Searls quote on identity ('MyTerms should not be dependent on a universal identity system') is the chair's opinion in a brainstorming post, not the standard's text. The standard's normative text was not read. The protocol-neutral claim rests on the official abstract ('any protocol that serves the purpose') and on the chair's account of the draft.

fieldFixes.correction: The standard does not specify a technology. Agents may use 'any protocol that serves the purpose', and the form of the shared record is left open. What it does require is that an agreed contract be signed electronically by both parties or their agents, and that both keep matching records. Header signalling, plug-ins, a transparency log and Doc Searls's 'MyTerms Agreement Record' are implementation ideas, not requirements. Searls, the working-group chair, says MyTerms should not depend on a universal identity system.
